001.summary: Game four of four at Alex's, three-player, and the only win of the night — the pilot calls it the funniest game of the year. He ramped through the early removal, the table spent its wipes on mid-tier dinosaurs, and because he rebuilt faster than they could answer he could fire Blasphemous Act into an empty board of his own to clear theirs at no cost. Gishath then connected on Stuart for 7, revealed 7 and hit five dinosaurs; Enlarge the next turn made it a 14-point swing onto Stuart's existing 7 commander damage for lethal. ONE CAVEAT: the entry's decklist_sha256 matches the current list, and Enlarge is not in that list — so either the paper deck differs from the tracked 99 or the finishing card is not one this list can draw.

cards.why: "revealed 7 cards off the trigger, hit FIVE dinosaurs", then 2 more off a 14-card reveal — the note's own framing is that the deck's actual threat is the commander and the trigger.
"when my board was empty I could fire BLASPHEMOUS ACT to clear THEIRS at no cost to me. That asymmetry was the whole game."

"+7/+7 on Gishath, swinging for 14 into Stuart's existing 7 commander damage = 21 and lethal by commander damage." Flagged: the note names it but it is not in the tracked 99 under this entry's own decklist_sha256.

decisions.spot: own board empty after the table's wraths, opponents redeveloped: fire Blasphemous Act now for the free one-sided wipe, or hold it and rebuild first

takeaways: In this one game the mid-tier dinosaurs effectively soaked the table's removal and the commander landed into an empty answer slate — the pilot's read is that the deck's actual threat is Gishath and its trigger, not the bodies that precede it.
Blasphemous Act's asymmetry window is an empty board of your own: in this game it cleared theirs at no cost and the pilot calls that asymmetry the whole game.
One of the revealed dinosaurs makes opposing creatures enter tapped, which the note says is why the board could not stabilise after the first connect — the reveal is not just bodies.
The pilot proposes no changes: he reads this single game as the deck working as designed. It is one logged game and a win, so nothing here is yet a pattern.

open_questions.question: Does the tracked 99 actually contain a pump effect that converts a Gishath connect into lethal commander damage, given that Enlarge — the card that finished this game — is not in the list this entry's decklist_sha256 points at?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The only logged win ends on a card the tracked list does not hold. Either the paper deck has drifted from the tracked 99 or the finishing line is not repeatable from this list, and the log cannot tell those apart.

002.summary: Second game of a 0-2 night at Alex's, four-player, 2.5-3 hours of "wipe after wipe". A turn-one Sol Ring and Arcane Signet made four mana, then the pilot was green-screwed for a long stretch with double-green dinos, Selvala and Rishkar's Expertise stranded in hand — which, by accident, kept his creatures out of the early wipe waves. Once green arrived Gishath came online, was pumped to a 16/16 and killed Tom with 16 commander damage on top of Tom's existing 7, breaking a no-attack deal with Oliver to do it (the pilot stands by that); the 16-card reveal hit only two dinos because the board had already been stormed by the third and fourth reveals of the game. Zacama (the note spells it Zakama) came down for 7 off Urza's Incubator, Swords to Plowshares landed on open mana, Alex's Walking Ballista went down and the pilot was back to 13 with the game "effectively won". The loss is a single sequencing error the pilot names as critical: 8-9 dinos with counters and 30+ power on board against Alex at 18 and Oliver at 15, he attacked only Oliver, Alex saved him, and Oliver drained the pilot out with a gain/lose/damage vampire spell. Cause filed as politics. The entry's decklist_sha256 matches the current list. The note's text also carries a two-game summary and a follow-ups line that belong to the Edgar game played the same night; that game is not this deck's and is not read here.

decisions.spot: 8-9 dinos with counters and 30+ power on board, Alex at 18 and Oliver at 15: swing everything at both seats, or attack only Oliver
Gishath is a 16/16 and Tom's board would wipe you if left alone: honour the no-attack deal with Oliver, or break it to kill Tom

takeaways: Close lethal when it is on the board — the pilot's own line is "hesitation cost the game": with 30+ power against 18 and 15, attacking only Oliver let Alex save him and the drain came back.
Audit green pip distribution and green sources in the mana base: a turn-one four-mana start still left Selvala, Rishkar's Expertise and the double-green dinos stranded for a long stretch.

In removal-heavy games, holding creatures back through the wipe waves is a real strategy and not just an accident — the screw did it for him this game and the board that came down afterwards was the one that mattered.
The enrage engine is idling — the pilot's read is too few ping sources to activate it, and that it is a better fit for Standard than Commander.

The pilot's own arc across the night: "the tuning has moved from 'rebuild the deck' to 'sequence and close better'" — a Gishath list that reached a won position and lost it to sequencing, not to what it drew.

open_questions.question: How often does this list have the green it needs on curve? The pilot asks for a green pip / green source audit after being stranded with double-green dinos, Selvala and Rishkar's Expertise despite a four-mana turn one. deck-facts reads green as the heaviest colour — 55 total pips across 39 cards — against 22 green land sources (26 with rocks and dorks) and a source target of 36; mana_analysis reads green on-curve at 0.639 lands-only and 0.742 with rocks and dorks. Does the goldfish's castability by turn for the GG cards agree with what the table showed, and what does a land pass buy?
open_questions.why_it_matters: the screw hid the creatures from the wipes this once, but a list whose commander needs {R}{G}{W} cannot rely on being unable to cast its green; mana-analysis and mana-fit are the deterministic evidence for any land swap

open_questions.question: Should the enrage package stay? The pilot reads it as idling — "too few ping sources to activate it; better fit for Standard than Commander." engine.json's conversion stage carries the enrage residue as two cards, Trapjaw Tyrant and Wrathful Raptors, with 'Enrage engine drawn' at 56.7% assembled, 28.1% by turn 6, and calls it thin; the pilot's word 'package' may cover more than those two. What does the deck lose by cutting it, and what would the slots buy — including toward closing lethal?
open_questions.why_it_matters: the note names it as a follow-up in its own words, and two logged games have now been decided by the commander's swing rather than by anything enrage did

open_questions.question: With 8-9 Dinosaurs carrying counters and 30+ power on board, Alex at 18 and Oliver at 15, was an alpha strike split across both seats lethal on Oliver even after Alex saves himself — and what does Alex's Azorius counters deck need to hold to stop it? The note gives only the totals, not the individual bodies.
open_questions.why_it_matters: the pilot files this as the critical error and the cause of the loss; a resolved board is what turns 'should have swung everything' into a spread the pilot can rehearse, and it is the closest thing this deck has to a lethal-swing scenario (engine.json notes no checker-passed stack resolves one)

open_questions.question: Is deliberately holding creatures in hand through a removal-heavy table's wipe waves — then deploying into the cleared board — a documented line against wrath-dense pods, and what does it cost a deck whose commander needs the board to do anything?
open_questions.why_it_matters: the pilot promotes it from accident to strategy on one game's evidence; the strategy DB either has this school or it does not
